910.name: Pre-Roman Italy and the Etruscans
910.description: The diverse pre-Roman cultures of the Italian peninsula: the mysterious Etruscan civilization, Greek colonies of Magna Graecia, and the Italic tribes, all of which contributed to the rise of Rome.

sub_clusters.name: Etruscan Civilization
sub_clusters.description: The Etruscan city-states of central Italy: their advanced metallurgy, art, religion, writing system, and profound influence on early Roman culture, governance, and engineering.

sub_clusters.name: Magna Graecia and Italic Peoples
sub_clusters.description: The Greek colonies of southern Italy and Sicily (Syracuse, Tarentum, Croton), the Italic tribal groups (Samnites, Latins, Umbrians), and the competitive cultural milieu that shaped early Rome.

910.name: The Roman Republic
910.description: The rise of the Roman Republic from a small city-state to the master of the Mediterranean: the struggle of the orders, the Punic Wars, expansion, civil wars, and the transformation into the Roman Empire.

sub_clusters.name: Early Republic and Italian Expansion
sub_clusters.description: The overthrow of the Etruscan kings, the establishment of the Republic, the Conflict of the Orders (patricians vs. plebeians), the Samnite Wars, and the unification of the Italian peninsula.

sub_clusters.name: Punic Wars and Mediterranean Dominance
sub_clusters.description: The three Punic Wars against Carthage: Hannibal's invasion across the Alps, Scipio Africanus's victory at Zama, the destruction of Carthage, and Rome's establishment as the supreme Mediterranean power.
key_events: Hannibal crosses the Alps and invades Italy (218 BC)
Battle of Zama — Scipio defeats Hannibal; Rome dominates the western Mediterranean (202 BC)

sub_clusters.name: Late Republic and Civil Wars
sub_clusters.description: The crisis of the Roman Republic: the Gracchi reforms, Marius's military reforms, Sulla's dictatorship, the Spartacus revolt, the First Triumvirate, Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon, his assassination, and Octavian's victory at Actium.
key_events: Julius Caesar crosses the Rubicon, igniting civil war (49 BC)
Assassination of Julius Caesar on the Ides of March (44 BC)

910.name: The Roman Empire
910.description: The Roman Empire from Augustus to the fall of Rome: the Pax Romana, the imperial system, Christianity's rise, the crisis of the third century, and the final collapse of Western Roman civilization.

sub_clusters.name: Augustus and the Pax Romana
sub_clusters.description: The Augustan settlement, the Julio-Claudian and Flavian dynasties, the 'Five Good Emperors,' the construction of the Colosseum, Trajan's Column, Hadrian's Wall, and two centuries of unprecedented peace and prosperity.
key_events: Octavian becomes Augustus, first Roman Emperor — the Principate begins (27 BC)
Colosseum completed in Rome under Titus (80 AD)

sub_clusters.name: Crisis, Christianity, and the Fall of Rome
sub_clusters.description: The Crisis of the Third Century, Diocletian's reforms, Constantine's conversion and the Edict of Milan, Theodosius and Christianity as state religion, the sack of Rome by Visigoths (410) and Vandals (455), and Odoacer's deposition of the last Western Emperor.
key_events: Edict of Milan — Constantine legalizes Christianity (313 AD)
Fall of the Western Roman Empire — Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus (476 AD)

920.name: Early Medieval Italy
920.description: Post-Roman Italy divided between Ostrogoths, Byzantines, Lombards, and the Papal States, Charlemagne's intervention, and the fragmentation that would define Italian political life for a millennium.

sub_clusters.name: Ostrogoths, Byzantines, and Lombards
sub_clusters.description: Odoacer and Theodoric's Ostrogothic Kingdom, Justinian's reconquest, the devastating Gothic Wars, the Lombard invasion and kingdom, and the emergence of the Papal States under Byzantine protection.

sub_clusters.name: Carolingian Italy and Fragmentation
sub_clusters.description: Charlemagne's conquest of the Lombard Kingdom, the Carolingian donation to the Papacy, the dissolution of Carolingian authority, Arab raids on Sicily and southern Italy, and the rise of local powers.

920.name: Medieval Communes and Maritime Republics
920.description: The flourishing of Italian medieval city-states, the Guelph-Ghibelline conflicts, the great maritime republics, the Papal-Imperial struggle, and the emergence of Renaissance culture.

sub_clusters.name: Communes and Guelph-Ghibelline Conflicts
sub_clusters.description: The emergence of self-governing communes in northern and central Italy, the Investiture Controversy, the Lombard League's victory at Legnano (1176), Dante's Florence, and the factional warfare between papal and imperial supporters.

sub_clusters.name: Maritime Republics — Venice, Genoa, Amalfi, Pisa
sub_clusters.description: The four great maritime republics that dominated Mediterranean trade: Venice's eastern empire, Genoa's Black Sea network, Amalfi's early commercial code, and Pisa's Tyrrhenian dominance.

sub_clusters.name: Papal States and Avignon Papacy
sub_clusters.description: The development of the Papal States as a temporal power, the Avignon 'Babylonian Captivity' of the Papacy (1309–1377), the Great Western Schism, and Cola di Rienzo's brief Roman Republic.

930.name: The Italian Renaissance
930.description: The extraordinary cultural, artistic, and intellectual flowering of the Italian Renaissance: the rebirth of classical learning, the patronage of the Medici, and the greatest concentration of artistic genius in human history.

sub_clusters.name: Florence and the Medici
sub_clusters.description: The rise of the Medici banking dynasty, their transformation of Florence into the cradle of the Renaissance, Cosimo and Lorenzo the Magnificent's patronage, Savonarola's bonfire of the vanities, and Machiavelli's political philosophy.
key_events: Lorenzo de' Medici 'the Magnificent' rules Florence at the peak of the Renaissance (1469–1492)

sub_clusters.name: Renaissance Art and Genius
sub_clusters.description: The unparalleled artistic achievement of the Italian Renaissance: Brunelleschi's dome, Botticelli, Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel and David, Raphael, Titian, and the development of perspective, anatomy, and naturalism.
key_events: Leonardo da Vinci paints The Last Supper (1495–1498)
Michelangelo completes the Sistine Chapel ceiling (1512)

sub_clusters.name: Italian Wars and Foreign Domination
sub_clusters.description: The Italian Wars (1494–1559): Charles VIII's invasion, the Sack of Rome (1527), the struggle between France and Spain for control of Italy, and the Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis establishing Spanish hegemony.

930.name: Spanish and Austrian Italy
930.description: Italy under Spanish Habsburg and later Austrian domination, the Counter-Reformation, Baroque culture, scientific revolution contributions (Galileo), and the gradual stirrings of reform and national consciousness.

sub_clusters.name: Spanish Habsburg Domination
sub_clusters.description: Spanish rule over Naples, Sicily, Sardinia, and Milan, the Counter-Reformation and Council of Trent, the Inquisition, Galileo's trial, Baroque art (Caravaggio, Bernini), and economic decline.

sub_clusters.name: Austrian Rule and Enlightenment Reforms
sub_clusters.description: The Treaty of Utrecht's transfer of Italian territories to Austria, Enlightenment reforms under Maria Theresa and Joseph II, the Kingdom of Sardinia-Piedmont's growing importance, and Cesare Beccaria's legal thought.

940.name: Risorgimento and Italian Unification
940.description: The Risorgimento (Resurgence): from Napoleon's disruption of the old order through decades of revolutionary struggle to the unification of Italy under the House of Savoy — one of the 19th century's defining national movements.

sub_clusters.name: Napoleonic Italy and Restoration
sub_clusters.description: Napoleon's conquest and reorganization of Italy, the brief taste of unity, the Congress of Vienna's restoration of the old order, the Carbonari secret societies, Mazzini's Young Italy, and the failed 1848 revolutions.

sub_clusters.name: Cavour, Garibaldi, and Unification
sub_clusters.description: Cavour's diplomatic genius, the alliance with Napoleon III, the wars against Austria, Garibaldi's Expedition of the Thousand and the conquest of the South, the proclamation of the Kingdom of Italy (1861), and the capture of Rome (1870).
key_events: Kingdom of Italy proclaimed with Victor Emmanuel II as king (March 17, 1861)
Italian forces capture Rome; completion of unification (September 20, 1870)

940.name: Liberal Italy and Colonial Ventures
940.description: United Italy's growing pains: the Southern Question, mass emigration, industrialization of the north, colonial ambitions in Africa (Libya, Ethiopia), the Giolittian era, and entry into World War I.

sub_clusters.name: Southern Question and Mass Emigration
sub_clusters.description: The stark economic divide between industrializing north and impoverished south, the massive wave of Italian emigration to the Americas (over 4 million by 1900), brigandage, and the social question.

sub_clusters.name: Colonial Ventures and Giolittian Era
sub_clusters.description: Italy's colonial ventures: the humiliating defeat at Adwa in Ethiopia (1896), the conquest of Libya from the Ottomans (1911–1912), Giolitti's liberal reforms, and the debate over entry into WWI.

950.name: World War I and the Rise of Fascism
950.description: Italy's brutal WWI experience, the 'mutilated victory,' social upheaval, the rise of Mussolini's Fascist movement, the March on Rome, and the creation of the totalitarian Fascist state.

sub_clusters.name: Italy in World War I
sub_clusters.description: Italy's entry into WWI on the Allied side (Treaty of London), the horrific Isonzo battles, the catastrophic defeat at Caporetto (1917), the recovery at Vittorio Veneto, and the 'mutilated victory' at the Paris Peace Conference.

sub_clusters.name: March on Rome and the Fascist State
sub_clusters.description: Post-war turmoil and the Biennio Rosso, Mussolini's March on Rome (1922), the Matteotti crisis, the construction of the totalitarian state, the Lateran Pacts with the Vatican, the conquest of Ethiopia (1935–1936), and the Axis alliance with Nazi Germany.
key_events: Mussolini's March on Rome — Fascist seizure of power (October 28, 1922)
Italy invades and conquers Ethiopia (1935–1936)

950.name: WWII and the Postwar Republic
950.description: Italy's disastrous WWII experience, the fall of Mussolini, the Italian resistance, the birth of the Republic, and the extraordinary postwar economic miracle that transformed Italy into a modern industrial power.

sub_clusters.name: Italy in World War II
sub_clusters.description: Italy's entry into WWII, military disasters in Greece and North Africa, the Allied invasion of Sicily, the fall of Mussolini (July 1943), the German occupation, the Salò Republic, the Italian resistance, and the Liberation.
key_events: Fall of Mussolini; Italy signs armistice with the Allies (July–September 1943)
Liberation Day — end of German occupation of Italy (April 25, 1945)

sub_clusters.name: Birth of the Republic and Economic Miracle
sub_clusters.description: The 1946 referendum establishing the Italian Republic, the democratic constitution, Marshall Plan reconstruction, the miracolo economico (1958–1963) that made Italy the world's sixth-largest economy, and Italy's role as a founding member of the EEC.

960.name: Years of Lead and Mafia Wars
960.description: Italy's turbulent late 20th century: left-wing and right-wing terrorism during the Anni di Piombo (Years of Lead), the Aldo Moro kidnapping, the Maxi Trial against the Sicilian Mafia, and the Tangentopoli corruption scandal.

sub_clusters.name: Anni di Piombo (Years of Lead)
sub_clusters.description: Two decades of political violence: the Hot Autumn of 1969, the Piazza Fontana bombing, the Bologna massacre (1980), the Red Brigades' kidnapping and murder of Prime Minister Aldo Moro (1978), and the strategy of tension.
key_events: Red Brigades kidnap and murder former PM Aldo Moro (1978)
Bologna train station bombing — deadliest terrorist attack in Italian history (August 2, 1980)

sub_clusters.name: Mafia Wars and Anti-Mafia Struggle
sub_clusters.description: The Second Mafia War in Sicily, the Maxi Trial organized by Judges Falcone and Borsellino, their assassinations in 1992, and the Italian state's intensified fight against organized crime.
key_events: Judges Giovanni Falcone and Paolo Borsellino assassinated by the Mafia (1992)

sub_clusters.name: Tangentopoli and Political Upheaval
sub_clusters.description: The Mani Pulite (Clean Hands) investigation that exposed systematic corruption, the collapse of the entire postwar party system (DC, PSI), and the transition to Italy's 'Second Republic.'

960.name: Contemporary Italy
960.description: Italy's Second Republic: the Berlusconi era, EU integration and the eurozone, economic stagnation, migration challenges, populist movements, and Italy's role in contemporary European politics.

sub_clusters.name: Berlusconi Era and the Second Republic
sub_clusters.description: Silvio Berlusconi's domination of Italian politics, his media empire, the alternation between center-right and center-left coalitions, constitutional reform attempts, and Italy's economic stagnation relative to EU partners.

sub_clusters.name: Economic Challenges and Populism
sub_clusters.description: The Monti technocratic government, the eurozone crisis, Renzi's reform agenda, the rise of the Five Star Movement and Lega, the Conte coalition, the COVID-19 crisis, Draghi's unity government, and Giorgia Meloni's government.
key_events: Giorgia Meloni becomes Italy's first female Prime Minister (October 2022)

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
